summary: The Hit points calculator returns single max hit pts eq from the 19 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Hit points calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hit points calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports single max hit pts eq in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the class, the level and the multiclass boxes (numbered 1 to 4)).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hit points calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Single max hit pts eq=((((class) > 0) ? ( constitution modifier × level + is hill dwarf × level + 2 × is tough × level + single points + (is draconic sorcerer × level) ) : ( constitution modifier × level + is hill dwarf × level + 2 × is tough × level + single points + (0) )))
Multi max hit pts eq=(constitution modifier × (((class, multiclass #1, multiclass #2, multiclass #3, multiclass #4, level, level in multiclass #1, level in multiclass #2, level in multiclass #3, level in multiclass #4))) + is draconic sorcerer × (((class, multiclass #1, multiclass #2, multiclass #3, multiclass #4, level, level in multiclass #1, level in multiclass #2, level in multiclass #3, level in multiclass #4))) + is hill dwarf × (((class, multiclass #1, multiclass #2, multiclass #3, multiclass #4, level, level in multiclass #1, level in multiclass #2, level in multiclass #3, level in multiclass #4))) + 2 × is tough × (((class, multiclass #1, multiclass #2, multiclass #3, multiclass #4, level, level in multiclass #1, level in multiclass #2, level in multiclass #3, level in multiclass #4))) + single points)
Is sorcerer=(class)
Is any sorcerer=(class, multiclass #1, multiclass #2, multiclass #3, multiclass #4)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hit points calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hit points calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns single max hit pts eq. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hit points calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (19 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Hit points calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
